title: AI Is Now Controlling Fusion Energy — Faster Than Any Human Could
summary:
Imagine trying to control something that changes faster than you can blink. That's what scientists face when working with fusion energy — the same power that makes the sun shine. The plasma inside a fusion machine can become unstable in just a few thousandths of a second. No human can react that fast!

So scientists at Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory came up with a clever solution: they trained artificial intelligence (AI) to do it. They call their system PACMAN (short for Prediction And Control using MAchiNe learning).

PACMAN is like a super-smart robot that watches the plasma all the time. It checks temperature, density, and magnetic signals. If it sees something going wrong, it can make a decision in about 20 milliseconds — that's 20 thousandths of a second! A human takes about a second to react. So PACMAN is about 50 times faster!

In one test, PACMAN predicted a problem called a "tearing mode" about 200 milliseconds before it happened. That gave the machine time to change the plasma and avoid the problem altogether. It's like stopping a car before it hits a pothole, instead of after.

PACMAN works like an assembly line. First, it collects data from the machine. Then it checks for errors. Next, AI models predict what the plasma will do. Then controllers decide what actions to take. Finally, it makes sure everything is safe and sends the commands.

The scientists tested PACMAN on a real fusion machine called DIII-D in San Diego, and it worked in five separate experiments. This is a big step toward making fusion energy practical — a clean, almost unlimited source of power.

So next time you hear about AI, remember: it's not just for playing games or writing stories. It might one day help power our world!
why_it_matters: When you turn on a light in the future, the electricity might come from fusion energy — and an AI like PACMAN could be one reason it works.

background_read: The sun shines because of fusion — the same process scientists are trying to recreate on Earth.
Plasma is an extremely hot, electrically charged gas, and keeping it steady inside a fusion machine is one of the hardest jobs in science.
PACMAN comes from Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, a U.S. research center, and was tested on DIII-D, a real fusion machine in San Diego.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and their AI system PACMAN.
WHAT: PACMAN spots dangerous plasma problems and fixes them in about 20 milliseconds — a speed no human could reach.
WHERE: On the DIII-D fusion machine in San Diego, where PACMAN was tested.
WHY: Fusion plasma breaks down too fast for people to react, so AI could be the key to making clean fusion power work.

perspectives.description: They are proud that their AI worked in five tests and believe it could help make fusion energy practical.
They know fusion power is still far away and want much more testing before AI is trusted with big, powerful machines.

perspectives.perspective: People who want clean energy for the future
perspectives.description: If fusion power works, it could mean a world with almost unlimited clean electricity — and AI may be the helper that gets us there.
